claim: maVie16 is a mouse-adapted SARS-CoV-2 virus generated by serial passaging of a human isolate (BavPat1) through BALB/c mice for 16 passages.
source: We generated maVie16, a mouse-adapted SARS-CoV-2, by serial passaging of a human isolate.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental procedure of serial passaging and presents data showing progressive adaptation (Figure 1).

claim: Only three Spike mutations in maVie16 enhanced interaction with murine ACE2 according to in silico modeling.
source: In silico modeling revealed how only three Spike mutations of maVie16 enhanced interaction with murine ACE2.
evidence: Structural modeling data presented in Figure 2 demonstrates the predicted interactions between mutated Spike residues and mACE2.

claim: maVie16 induced profound pathology in BALB/c and C57BL/6 mice.
source: maVie16 induced profound pathology in BALB/c and C57BL/6 mice
evidence: Experimental data showing weight loss, temperature changes, and histological pathology in both mouse strains (Figures 3, 5).

claim: mCOVID-19 replicated critical aspects of human disease, including early lymphopenia, pulmonary immune cell infiltration, pneumonia, and specific adaptive immunity.
source: the resulting mouse COVID-19 (mCOVID-19) replicated critical aspects of human disease, including early lymphopenia, pulmonary immune cell infiltration, pneumonia, and specific adaptive immunity.
evidence: Flow cytometry data showing lymphopenia (Figure 4A), immune cell infiltration (Figure 4C), histological evidence of pneumonia (Figure 5C), and antibody responses (Figure 5E).

claim: Inhibition of IFNγ and TNF substantially reduced immunopathology in maVie16-infected mice.
source: Inhibition of the proinflammatory cytokines IFNγ and TNF substantially reduced immunopathology.
evidence: Experimental data showing reduced weight loss and lung weights in antibody-treated mice (Figure 6E, G).

claim: Genetic ACE2-deficiency completely prevented mCOVID-19 development.
source: Importantly, genetic ACE2-deficiency completely prevented mCOVID-19 development.
evidence: Data from Ace2-/y mice showing maintained body weight, temperature, and absence of lung pathology (Figure 7B-E).

claim: Inhalation therapy with recombinant ACE2 fully protected mice from mCOVID-19.
source: Finally, inhalation therapy with recombinant ACE2 fully protected mice from mCOVID-19, revealing a novel and efficient treatment.
evidence: Experimental data showing protection from weight loss, reduced viral load, and improved survival with rmsACE2 treatment (Figure 7G-O).

claim: Disease severity is determined by cytokine-driven immunopathology and critically dependent on ACE2 in vivo.
source: disease severity is determined by cytokine-driven immunopathology and critically dependent on ACE2 in vivo.
evidence: Combined evidence from cytokine blocking experiments (Figure 6) and ACE2 knockout experiments (Figure 7).

claim: The Q498H mutation appeared immediately after passage 1 and correlated with early increase in viral load.
source: Most prominently, we observed the immediate appearance of Q498H after passage 1 (Figure 2B), which correlated with the early increase in viral load (and hence viral propagation) in infected mice (Figure 1B).
evidence: Sequencing data showing mutation appearance (Figure 2B) and viral load measurements (Figure 1B).

claim: The Q493R mutation was detected after passage 12.
source: After passage 12, we detected a glutamine to arginine exchange at position Q493R (Figure 2B).
evidence: Sequencing data presented in Figure 2B showing mutation dynamics.

claim: Mutations at Q493 and Q498 have been reported in other mouse-adapted SARS-CoV-2 strains.
source: Importantly, mutations at Q493 and Q498 have been also reported in other mouse-adapted SARS-CoV-2 strains (Dinnon et al., 2020; Huang et al., 2021; Leist et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020b), suggesting a critical role in Spike adaptation to the murine ACE2 receptor.
evidence: Citations to previous studies reporting similar mutations.

claim: Q493 and Q498 mutations were detected in the Omicron/B.1.1.529 variant for the first time in a human SARS-CoV-2 variant.
source: With the appearance of Omicron/B.1.1.529, the most recent VOC, Q493, and Q498 mutations were detected in a human SARS-CoV-2 variant for the first time.
evidence: Reference to the emergence of Omicron variant with these mutations.

claim: Mutations in K417 appeared around passage 10 and have been reported in Omicron/B.1.1.529, Beta/B.1.351, and Gamma/P1 variants.
source: Mutations in K417 (which appeared around passage 10; Figure 2B) have also been reported in Omicron/B.1.1.529 and two other human VOCs, that is, Beta/B.1.351 (K417N) (Tegally et al., 2020) and Gamma/P1 (K417T) (Voloch, 2020).
evidence: Sequencing data (Figure 2B) and citations to variant characterization studies.

claim: The surface of mACE2 consists of more negatively charged amino acids than hACE2.
source: Structural analyses of mouse and human ACE2 (mACE2 and hACE2, respectively) have shown that the surface of mACE2 consists of more negative charged amino acids than that of hACE2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A; Rodrigues et al., 2020).
evidence: Structural modeling data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) and citation to previous structural analysis.

claim: The maVie16 Spike Q498H mutation strengthens interaction with mACE2 at amino acid D38.
source: Detailed structural modeling of the BavPat1 versus the maVie16 Spike protein interface with mACE2 revealed that the maVie16 Spike Q498H mutation would strengthen its interaction with mACE2 at amino acid D38, otherwise forming an intramolecular salt bridge with mACE2 H353 (Figure 2D).
evidence: Structural modeling predictions shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The arginine at maVie16 Spike position 493 is predicted to interact with the negatively charged mACE2 amino acid E35.
source: Similarly, the newly introduced arginine at maVie16 Spike position 493 is predicted to efficiently interact with the negatively charged mACE2 amino acid E35, thus further stabilizing the maVie16 Spike/mACE2 interaction by neutralizing the otherwise unpaired negative charge of mACE2 glutamic acid (Figure 2D).
evidence: Structural modeling predictions shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The threonine at Spike position 417 (T417) of maVie16 is predicted to enhance interaction with asparagine at position 30 of mACE2.
source: Finally, the threonine at Spike position 417 (T417) of maVie16's is predicted to enhance the interaction with the neutrally charged asparagine at position 30 of mACE2 while the aspartic acid at this position in hACE2 forms a salt bridge with lysine K417 of the original BavPat1 isolate.
evidence: Structural modeling predictions discussed in the text.

claim: maVie16 showed similar propagation kinetics in Vero and Caco-2 cells as compared to BavPat1.
source: Of note, maVie16 showed similar propagation kinetics in Vero and Caco-2 cells as compared to BavPat1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: In vitro viral propagation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: In BALB/c mice, maVie16 at 4 × 10³ TCID50 caused profound weight loss starting around day 3 post infection.
source: In BALB/c mice, maVie16 was highly pathogenic and caused profound weight loss, starting around day 3 post infection (p.i.) at a dose of 4 × 103 TCID50 (Figure 3A)
evidence: Body weight data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: All tested higher doses than 4 × 10³ TCID50 in BALB/c mice caused earlier weight loss (day 2 p.i.) and lethality starting at day 4 p.i.
source: whereas all tested higher doses caused an earlier weight loss (day 2 p.i.) and lethality starting at day 4 p.i. (Figure 3B).
evidence: Survival and body weight data shown in Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: Loss of body weight correlated with hypothermia in BALB/c mice infected with maVie16.
source: Notably, the loss of body weight correlated with hypothermia (Figure 3C).
evidence: Body temperature data shown in Figure 3C correlating with weight loss data.

claim: maVie16 infection did not cause lethality nor significant hypothermia in C57BL/6 animals.
source: In contrast to BALB/c mice, maVie16 infection did not cause lethality nor significant hypothermia in C57BL/6 animals
evidence: Survival and temperature data for C57BL/6 mice shown in Figures 3E and 3F.

claim: 1 × 10⁵ TCID50 maVie16 induced profound but transient body weight loss of about 15% in C57BL/6 mice.
source: albeit 1 × 105 (and higher) TCID50 induced a profound but transient body weight loss of about 15% (Figure 3D–F).
evidence: Body weight data for C57BL/6 mice shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Both BALB/c and C57BL/6 mouse strains infected with 1 × 10⁵ TCID50 showed similar body weight loss (approximately 15%) at day 3 p.i.
source: Interestingly, both mouse strains infected with 1 × 105 TCID50 showed similar body weight loss (approximately 15%) at day 3 p.i., but while disease severity further increased in BALB/c animals, C57BL/6 mice recovered.
evidence: Comparison of body weight data between strains from Figure 3.

claim: BALB/c animals showed more severe lung pathologies compared to C57BL/6 mice at day 3 post infection.
source: In line with these data, BALB/c animals showed more severe lung pathologies compared to C57BL/6 mice, as revealed by histological analyses of lungs on day 3 (Figure 3G and H).
evidence: Histological images and scoring data shown in Figures 3G, H, and I.

claim: Diffuse alveolar damage, characterized by alveolar collapse and septal thickening, was more pronounced in BALB/c mice than C57BL/6 mice.
source: While the cumulative histological score revealed no differences between the strains, diffuse alveolar damage, characterized by alveolar collapse and septal thickening, was more pronounced in BALB/c mice (Figure 3I).
evidence: Histological scoring data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: KRT18-hACE2 mice were most sensitive to BavPat1 infection and succumbed to infections at doses of 1 × 10³ or 1 × 10⁴ TCID50.
source: As expected (Oladunni et al., 2020), KRT18-hACE2 mice were most sensitive to infection and succumbed to BavPat1 infections (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Survival data for KRT18-hACE2 mice shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: BavPat1-infected KRT18-hACE2 mice appeared healthy until day 4 p.i. and then progressively lost weight until day 7, accompanied by hypothermia and death.
source: However, the disease course was profoundly different to that of maVie16-infected wild-type animals. BavPat1-infected KRT18-hACE2 mice appeared healthy until day 4 p.i. and then progressively lost weight until day 7, accompanied by hypothermia and death (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–F).
evidence: Body weight and temperature data for KRT18-hACE2 mice shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C-F.

claim: Death in KRT18-hACE2 mice most likely results from severe encephalitis due to expression of hACE2 in neurons where ACE2 is normally not expressed.
source: Death in KRT18-hACE2 mice most likely results from severe encephalitis due to expression of hACE2 in neurons where ACE2 is normally not expressed (Hikmet et al., 2020).
evidence: Citation to study on ACE2 expression patterns.

claim: maVie16 infection caused severe blood leukopenia on day 2 p.i. with prominent reduction of lymphocytes, monocytes, neutrophils, and NK cells.
source: maVie16 (5 × 105 TCID50) infection caused severe blood leukopenia on day 2 p.i. with a prominent reduction of lymphocytes, monocytes, neutrophils, and NK cells (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Flow cytometry data showing blood cell populations in Figure 4A and supplements.

claim: An expansion of peripheral plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDCs) was observed at day 2 p.i.
source: At the same time, we observed an expansion of peripheral plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDCs) (Figure 4B), which are important antiviral effector cells capable of efficient and rapid type I IFN production (Swiecki and Colonna, 2015).
evidence: Flow cytometry data showing pDC expansion in Figure 4B and citation to pDC function.

claim: Infection led to substantial pulmonary infiltration with leukocytes paralleling the development of pneumonia.
source: Infection led to substantial pulmonary infiltration with leukocytes (Figure 4C), paralleling the development of pneumonia.
evidence: Flow cytometry data showing lung leukocyte numbers in Figure 4C.

claim: A remarkable infiltration with pDCs in the lungs occurred on day 2 p.i.
source: A closer look at the inflammatory cell composition in the lungs revealed a remarkable infiltration with pDCs on day 2 p.i. (Figure 4C).
evidence: Flow cytometry data showing lung pDC numbers in Figure 4C.

claim: Conventional dendritic cells (cDCs) transiently accumulated in the lung on day 5 p.i.
source: Conventional dendritic cells (cDCs) transiently accumulated in the lung on day 5 p.i., followed by T helper and cytotoxic T cell infiltration and recruitment of monocytes on day 7 (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Flow cytometry data showing lung cDC numbers in Figure 4C.

claim: T helper and cytotoxic T cell infiltration and recruitment of monocytes occurred on day 7 p.i.
source: Conventional dendritic cells (cDCs) transiently accumulated in the lung on day 5 p.i., followed by T helper and cytotoxic T cell infiltration and recruitment of monocytes on day 7 (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Flow cytometry data showing lung T cell and monocyte numbers in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Lung neutrophil numbers dropped around day 2 p.i. to return to baseline levels over the remaining disease course.
source: The abundance of other analyzed immune cell populations did not change substantially, and lung neutrophil numbers dropped around day 2 p.i. to return to baseline levels over the remaining disease course (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Flow cytometry data showing lung neutrophil numbers in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Pulmonary NK cells did not significantly expand in the lungs of maVie16 infected C57BL6 mice.
source: Surprisingly, pulmonary NK cells, which fulfill important antiviral functions (Björkström et al., 2021), did not significantly expand in the lungs of maVie16 infected C57BL6 mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Flow cytometry data showing lung NK cell numbers in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and citation to NK cell function.

claim: Rapid induction of type I IFN-inducible genes (Eif2ak2 and ifit1) occurred in line with early lung pDC accumulation.
source: In line with an early lung pDC accumulation, we found rapid induction of type I IFN-inducible genes, such as Eif2ak2 (protein kinase R/PKR) and ifit1, accompanied by a profound Il6 response
evidence: Gene expression data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: A profound Il6 response accompanied the induction of type I IFN-inducible genes.
source: In line with an early lung pDC accumulation, we found rapid induction of type I IFN-inducible genes, such as Eif2ak2 (protein kinase R/PKR) and ifit1, accompanied by a profound Il6 response
evidence: Gene expression data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The expression of Tnf, Il10, Il1b, and Tgfb peaked between day 5 and 7 p.i.
source: the expression of Tnf, Il10, Il1b, and Tgfb peaked between day 5 and 7 p.i. (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Gene expression data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Ifng induction reached a maximum on day 7, coinciding with increased numbers of T cells.
source: The Ifng induction reached a maximum on day 7, coinciding with the increased numbers of T cells that are prominent sources of IFNγ (Figure 4D).
evidence: Gene expression data (Figure 4D) and T cell numbers (Figure 4C) showing temporal correlation.

claim: Lung weights significantly increased by day 5–7 p.i. in C57BL/6 mice infected with maVie16 (5 × 10⁵ TCID50).
source: In C57BL/6 mice infected with maVie16 (5 × 105 TCID50), lung weights significantly increased by day 5–7 p.i. (Figure 5A).
evidence: Lung weight data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Lung viral titers peaked at day 2 p.i. and then gradually declined.
source: Lung viral titers peaked at day 2 p.i. and then gradually declined (Figure 5B).
evidence: Viral load data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Immunohistochemical staining for SARS-CoV-2 nucleoprotein confirmed the initial presence and subsequent elimination of viral particles.
source: Immunohistochemical staining for SARS-CoV-2 nucleoprotein on lung slides confirmed the initial presence and subsequent elimination of viral particles (Figure 5C).
evidence: Immunohistochemistry images shown in Figure 5C showing viral nucleoprotein over time.

claim: Histological analyses revealed progressive interstitial and perivascular infiltration and signs of diffuse alveolar damage, peaking from day 5–7, and resolving by day 14 p.i.
source: Histological analyses of lung tissue revealed progressive interstitial and perivascular infiltration and signs of diffuse alveolar damage, such as alveolar collapse and septal thickening, peaking from day 5–7, and resolving by day 14 p.i. (Figure 5C).
evidence: Histological images and scoring data shown in Figures 5C and 5D.

claim: Vasculitis was observed early after infection (day 2) and resolved at later time points.
source: Interestingly, vasculitis was observed early after infection (day 2) and resolved at later time points (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: Histological observations shown in Figures 5C and 5D.

claim: Most acute inflammatory parameters had returned close to baseline at day 14 p.i., confirming resolution of inflammation.
source: Moreover, most acute inflammatory parameters (including cytokine genes, innate immune cells, and lung tissue weights) had returned close to baseline at day 14 p.i. (Figures 4 and 5A–D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2), confirming resolution of inflammation.
evidence: Multiple data types (cytokine expression, immune cell numbers, lung weights) shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Expansion of pulmonary cDCs and T helper cells occurred by day 5 and 7, indicating onset of adaptive immunity.
source: Onset of adaptive immunity, as indicated by expansion of pulmonary cDCs and T helper cells by day 5s and 7 (Figure 4C), as well as by increased spleen weight on day 7 p.i. (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D)
evidence: Flow cytometry data showing cDC and T cell expansion in Figure 4C.

claim: Increased spleen weight on day 7 p.i. indicated onset of adaptive immunity.
source: Onset of adaptive immunity, as indicated by expansion of pulmonary cDCs and T helper cells by day 5s and 7 (Figure 4C), as well as by increased spleen weight on day 7 p.i. (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D)
evidence: Spleen weight data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Significantly increased levels of anti-SARS-CoV-2 Spike protein-specific plasma IgG1, IgG2b, and IgA antibodies were detected on day 14 p.i.
source: was followed by an efficient humoral immune response, reflected by significantly increased levels of anti-SARS-CoV-2 Spike protein-specific plasma IgG1, IgG2b, and IgA antibodies on day 14 p.i. (Figure 5E).
evidence: ELISA data showing antibody titers in Figure 5E.

claim: Both BALB/c and C57BL/6 mouse strains exhibited a decline in blood leukocytes, including lymphocytes and NK cells, upon infections with maVie16.
source: Both mouse strains exhibited a decline in blood leukocytes, including lymphocytes and NK cells, upon infections with maVie16 (Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Flow cytometry data comparing strains shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Pulmonary immune cell dynamics did not differ between BALB/c and C57BL/6 strains, except for an expansion of NK cells in BALB/c mice and elevated pDC numbers in C57BL/6 animals.
source: Also, pulmonary immune cell dynamics did not differ between the strains, except for an expansion of NK cells in BALB/c mice, and elevated pDC numbers in C57BL/6 animals (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Flow cytometry data comparing lung immune cells between strains in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Higher NK cell abundance correlated with increased pulmonary IFNγ levels in BALB/c mice.
source: Higher NK cell abundance correlated with increased pulmonary IFNγ levels in BALB/c mice, whereas Il1b was slightly higher in C57BL/6 animals 3 days after infection (Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: NK cell numbers (Figure 6B) and IFNγ gene expression (Figure 6C) data showing correlation.

claim: Il1b was slightly higher in C57BL/6 animals compared to BALB/c mice 3 days after infection.
source: Higher NK cell abundance correlated with increased pulmonary IFNγ levels in BALB/c mice, whereas Il1b was slightly higher in C57BL/6 animals 3 days after infection (Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Gene expression data comparing strains shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Plasma cytokine levels, viral loads, spleen weight, and lung weight were comparable between BALB/c and C57BL/6 mouse strains at day 3 post infection.
source: Plasma cytokine levels (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D), viral loads (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E), as well as spleen and lung weight (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F) were comparable between the two mouse strains.
evidence: Multiple measurements shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D-F showing no significant differences.

claim: maVie16-infected BALB/c mice treated with anti-IFNγ and anti-TNF antibodies significantly improved weight loss.
source: maVie16-infected (1 × 105 TCID50) BALB/c mice treated intraperitoneally with a mixture of anti-IFNγ and anti-TNF antibodies (on days 1 and 3 p.i.; Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A) significantly improved weight loss (Figure 6E)
evidence: Body weight data from antibody treatment experiment shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Anti-IFNγ and anti-TNF antibody treatment decreased lung weights in maVie16-infected BALB/c mice.
source: maVie16-infected (1 × 105 TCID50) BALB/c mice treated intraperitoneally with a mixture of anti-IFNγ and anti-TNF antibodies (on days 1 and 3 p.i.; Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A) significantly improved weight loss (Figure 6E) and decreased lung weights (Figure 6G)
evidence: Lung weight data from antibody treatment experiment shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Anti-IFNγ and anti-TNF antibody treatment decreased viral load in maVie16-infected BALB/c mice.
source: maVie16-infected (1 × 105 TCID50) BALB/c mice treated intraperitoneally with a mixture of anti-IFNγ and anti-TNF antibodies (on days 1 and 3 p.i.; Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A) significantly improved weight loss (Figure 6E) and decreased lung weights (Figure 6G), the viral load (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B)
evidence: Viral load data from antibody treatment experiment shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Anti-IFNγ and anti-TNF antibody treatment decreased circulating monocyte levels in maVie16-infected BALB/c mice.
source: maVie16-infected (1 × 105 TCID50) BALB/c mice treated intraperitoneally with a mixture of anti-IFNγ and anti-TNF antibodies (on days 1 and 3 p.i.; Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A) significantly improved weight loss (Figure 6E) and decreased lung weights (Figure 6G), the viral load (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B), as well as circulating monocyte levels (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C)
evidence: Blood monocyte data from antibody treatment experiment shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Anti-IFNγ and anti-TNF antibody treatment had only minor effects on body temperature in BALB/c mice.
source: maVie16-infected (1 × 105 TCID50) BALB/c mice treated intraperitoneally with a mixture of anti-IFNγ and anti-TNF antibodies (on days 1 and 3 p.i.; Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A) significantly improved weight loss (Figure 6E) and decreased lung weights (Figure 6G), the viral load (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B), as well as circulating monocyte levels (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C) while it had only minor effects on body temperature (Figure 6F).
evidence: Body temperature data from antibody treatment experiment shown in Figure 6F.

claim: In C57BL/6 mice, anti-IFNγ and anti-TNF antibody treatment had no effects on body or lung weights, or viral load.
source: In C57BL/6 mice, the same treatment had no effects on body or lung weights, or viral load (Figure 6—figure supplement 2D, E, G and H)
evidence: Body weight, lung weight, and viral load data from C57BL/6 antibody treatment experiment shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2D, E, G, and H.

claim: In C57BL/6 mice, anti-IFNγ and anti-TNF antibody treatment significantly improved the altered body temperature and circulating leukocyte numbers.
source: In C57BL/6 mice, the same treatment had no effects on body or lung weights, or viral load (Figure 6—figure supplement 2D, E, G and H), but significantly improved the altered body temperature and circulating leukocyte numbers (Figure 6—figure supplement 2F and I).
evidence: Body temperature and blood leukocyte data from C57BL/6 antibody treatment experiment shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2F and I.

claim: ACE2 is essential for in vivo SARS-CoV infections.
source: We have previously shown (using Ace2 mutant mice) that ACE2 is essential for in vivo SARS-CoV infections (Kuba et al., 2005).
evidence: Citation to previous study using ACE2-deficient mice.

claim: Ace2-/y mice were fully protected against infection with 5 × 10⁵ TCID50 maVie16.
source: In contrast to infected littermate control animals, Ace2-/y mice were fully protected against infection with 5 × 105 TCID50 maVie16, maintained stable body weight (Figure 7B) and temperature (Figure 7C)
evidence: Body weight and temperature data from Ace2-/y mice shown in Figures 7B and 7C.

claim: Ace2-/y mice were protected from pneumonia development as indicated by lower lung weight and absence of lung pathology.
source: Ace2-/y mice were fully protected against infection with 5 × 105 TCID50 maVie16, maintained stable body weight (Figure 7B) and temperature (Figure 7C), and were protected from pneumonia development as indicated by lower lung weight (Figure 7D) and the absence of any lung pathology (Figure 7E).
evidence: Lung weight data (Figure 7D) and histological images (Figure 7E) from Ace2-/y mice.

claim: Complete absence of nucleocapsid-positive cells was observed in lungs of Ace2-/y animals.
source: Resistance to infection was further indicated by the complete absence of nucleocapsid-positive cells in lungs of Ace2-/y animals (Figure 7E).
evidence: Immunohistochemistry images showing no viral nucleoprotein in Ace2-/y mice in Figure 7E.

claim: Similar viral genome copy numbers were detected in both Ace2+/y and Ace2-/y mice, suggesting detection of initial maVie16 input rather than productive infection.
source: In conflict with this observation, we still detected similar viral genome copy numbers in both groups (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that this was reflective of initial maVie16 input rather than productive infection.
evidence: Viral genome copy number data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: maVie16-infected BALB/c mice treated with rmsACE2 did not lose body weight.
source: maVie16-infected (1 × 105 TCID50) BALB/c mice that were treated with rmsACE2 (Figure 7F and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C) did not lose body weight (Figure 7G)
evidence: Body weight data from rmsACE2 treatment experiment shown in Figure 7G.

claim: rmsACE2-treated BALB/c mice developed less hypothermia compared to vehicle-treated animals.
source: maVie16-infected (1 × 105 TCID50) BALB/c mice that were treated with rmsACE2 (Figure 7F and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C) did not lose body weight (Figure 7G), developed less hypothermia (Figure 7H)
evidence: Body temperature data from rmsACE2 treatment experiment shown in Figure 7H.

claim: rmsACE2-treated BALB/c mice exhibited lower lung weights compared to vehicle-treated animals.
source: maVie16-infected (1 × 105 TCID50) BALB/c mice that were treated with rmsACE2 (Figure 7F and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C) did not lose body weight (Figure 7G), developed less hypothermia (Figure 7H), exhibited lower lung weights (Figure 7I)
evidence: Lung weight data from rmsACE2 treatment experiment shown in Figure 7I.

claim: rmsACE2-treated BALB/c mice were largely protected from pneumonia.
source: maVie16-infected (1 × 105 TCID50) BALB/c mice that were treated with rmsACE2 (Figure 7F and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C) did not lose body weight (Figure 7G), developed less hypothermia (Figure 7H), exhibited lower lung weights (Figure 7I), and were largely protected from pneumonia (day 5 p.i.; Figure 7J)
evidence: Histological images from rmsACE2 treatment experiment shown in Figure 7J.

claim: rmsACE2-treated BALB/c mice had lower lung viral loads compared to vehicle-treated animals.
source: maVie16-infected (1 × 105 TCID50) BALB/c mice that were treated with rmsACE2 (Figure 7F and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C) did not lose body weight (Figure 7G), developed less hypothermia (Figure 7H), exhibited lower lung weights (Figure 7I), and were largely protected from pneumonia (day 5 p.i.; Figure 7J), had lower lung viral loads (Figure 7K)
evidence: Viral load data from rmsACE2 treatment experiment shown in Figure 7K.

claim: rmsACE2-treated BALB/c mice had fewer blood neutrophils compared to vehicle-treated animals.
source: maVie16-infected (1 × 105 TCID50) BALB/c mice that were treated with rmsACE2 (Figure 7F and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C) did not lose body weight (Figure 7G), developed less hypothermia (Figure 7H), exhibited lower lung weights (Figure 7I), and were largely protected from pneumonia (day 5 p.i.; Figure 7J), had lower lung viral loads (Figure 7K), and fewer blood neutrophils (Figure 7L) than vehicle-treated animals
evidence: Blood neutrophil data from rmsACE2 treatment experiment shown in Figure 7L.

claim: Fewer SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid-positive cells were found in lungs of BALB/c animals treated with rmsACE2 compared to controls.
source: Further, we found fewer SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid-positive cells in lungs of BALB/c animals treated with rmsACE2 5 days after infection with maVie16 as compared to controls (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Immunohistochemistry images from rmsACE2 treatment experiment shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D.

claim: rmsACE2 treatment of maVie16-infected C57BL/6 mice prevented weight loss and reduced viral load.
source: Similarly, rmsACE2 treatment of maVie16-infected (5 × 105 TCID50) C57BL/6 mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E) prevented weight loss and reduced the viral load (Figure 7—figure supplement 1F and G, respectively)
evidence: Body weight and viral load data from C57BL/6 rmsACE2 treatment experiment shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1F and G.

claim: rmsACE2 treatment did not affect temperature, lung weight, and blood leukocyte numbers in C57BL/6 mice.
source: Similarly, rmsACE2 treatment of maVie16-infected (5 × 105 TCID50) C57BL/6 mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E) prevented weight loss and reduced the viral load (Figure 7—figure supplement 1F and G, respectively) while it did not affect temperature, lung weight, and blood leukocyte numbers (Figure 7—figure supplement 1G, H and J, respectively).
evidence: Temperature, lung weight, and blood leukocyte data from C57BL/6 rmsACE2 treatment experiment shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1G, H, and J.

claim: Inhalative ACE2 therapy was fully protective when applied 12 hr post infection.
source: Strikingly, inhalative ACE2 therapy was still fully protective when applied 12 hr post infection (Figure 7M–O).
evidence: Body weight and survival data from delayed treatment experiment shown in Figure 7N and O.

claim: Mice that received inhalation therapy at 24 hr or 48 hr post infection still developed disease but mortality was completely prevented or reduced.
source: While mice that received inhalation therapy at later time points post infection still developed disease (Figure 7N), mortality was completely prevented or reduced when inhalative treatment was applied 24 hr or 48 hr post infection, respectively (Figure 7O).
evidence: Body weight and survival data from delayed treatment experiment shown in Figure 7N and O.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 was identified as the causative agent of COVID-19 in December 2019.
source: SARS-CoV-2 was identified as the causative agent of COVID-19 in December 2019
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about the origin of COVID-19.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 has infected 200 million people and caused 4.3 million confirmed deaths worldwide as of August 5, 2021.
source: SARS-CoV-2 was identified as the causative agent of COVID-19 in December 2019 and has since (until August 5, 2021) infected 200 million people and caused 4.3 million confirmed deaths worldwide (WHO, 2021b).
evidence: Citation to WHO data on COVID-19 statistics.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 evolution gave rise to multiple variants including novel variants of concern (VOCs) characterized by increased transmissibility and/or virulence, or reduced effectiveness of countermeasures.
source: Upon adaptation to humans, SARS-CoV-2 evolution gave rise to multiple variants including novel SARS-CoV-2 variants of concern (VOCs), characterized by increased transmissibility and/or virulence, or reduced effectiveness of countermeasures such as vaccinations or antibody therapies (WHO, 2021a).
evidence: Citation to WHO information on variants of concern.

claim: Clinical symptoms upon SARS-CoV-2 infection show a wide range, from asymptomatic disease to critical illness.
source: Clinical symptoms upon SARS-CoV-2 infection show a wide range, from asymptomatic disease to critical illness (Chen et al., 2020; Paranjpe et al., 2020).
evidence: Citations to clinical studies describing COVID-19 symptom spectrum.

claim: Severe COVID-19 is characterized by progressive respiratory failure, often necessitating hospitalization and mechanical ventilation.
source: Severe COVID-19 is characterized by progressive respiratory failure, often necessitating hospitalization and mechanical ventilation.
evidence: Established clinical knowledge about severe COVID-19.

claim: Fatal COVID-19 disease is linked to acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), associated with activation of inflammation and thrombosis, often resulting in multiorgan failure.
source: Fatal disease is linked to acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), associated with activation of inflammation and thrombosis, often resulting in multiorgan failure (Chen et al., 2020; Paranjpe et al., 2020).
evidence: Citations to clinical studies describing fatal COVID-19 pathology.

claim: Age, male sex, diabetes, and obesity have been found to be associated with the development of severe COVID-19.
source: Epidemiologically, several risk factors, such as age, male sex, diabetes, and obesity, have been found to be associated with the development of severe COVID-19 (Richardson et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2020).
evidence: Citations to epidemiological studies identifying risk factors.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 replicates primarily in nasopharyngeal and type II alveolar epithelial cells in the lower respiratory tract.
source: While SARS-CoV-2 replicates primarily in nasopharyngeal and type II alveolar epithelial cells in the lower respiratory tract, recent data point towards a broader cellular tropism under certain conditions (Sungnak et al., 2020; Ziegler, 2020).
evidence: Citations to studies on SARS-CoV-2 cellular tropism.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 cellular tropism largely correlates with ACE2 expression and TMPRSS2 expression.
source: This largely correlates with angiotensin-converting enzyme-2 (ACE2) expression, the entry receptor for SARS-CoV-2 (Hoffmann et al., 2020), and TMPRSS2 expression, a protease, which supports viral cell entry (Hoffmann et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2021; Murgolo et al., 2021).
evidence: Citations to studies on ACE2 and TMPRSS2 roles in viral entry.

claim: ACE2 is the entry receptor for SARS-CoV-2.
source: This largely correlates with angiotensin-converting enzyme-2 (ACE2) expression, the entry receptor for SARS-CoV-2 (Hoffmann et al., 2020)
evidence: Citation to study demonstrating ACE2 as SARS-CoV-2 receptor.

claim: TMPRSS2 is a protease that supports SARS-CoV-2 viral cell entry.
source: and TMPRSS2 expression, a protease, which supports viral cell entry (Hoffmann et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2021; Murgolo et al., 2021).
evidence: Citations to studies on TMPRSS2 function in viral entry.

claim: Severe COVID-19 disease seems to be driven by a circuit of T cells and macrophages causing a cytokine release syndrome, immunothrombosis, and resulting tissue damage that resembles macrophage activation syndrome.
source: Severe disease seems to be driven by a circuit of T cells and macrophages causing a cytokine release syndrome, immunothrombosis, and resulting tissue damage that resembles macrophage activation syndrome (Mangalmurti and Hunter, 2020).
evidence: Citation to study describing immunopathology in severe COVID-19.

claim: IFNγ released by T cells drives the emergence of pathologically activated, hyperinflammatory monocytes and macrophages that produce large amounts of IL-6, TNFα, and IL-1β.
source: As such, IFNγ released by T cells drives the emergence of pathologically activated, hyperinflammatory monocytes and macrophages that produce large amounts of interleukin (IL)-6, TNFα, and IL-1β (Grant et al., 2021).
evidence: Citation to study describing IFNγ-driven immunopathology.

claim: Mice are resistant to SARS-CoV-2 infection due to phylogenetic differences in ACE2.
source: Notably, mice are resistant to SARS-CoV-2 infection due to phylogenetic differences in ACE2 (Damas et al., 2020; Parolin et al., 2021).
evidence: Citations to studies explaining mouse resistance to SARS-CoV-2.

claim: KRT18-hACE2 transgenic mice express human ACE2 under the epithelial cytokeratin-18 (KRT18) promoter.
source: To circumvent the missing sensitivity of conventional mice, some groups studying SARS-CoV-2-related immune mechanisms take advantage of KRT18-hACE2 transgenic mice, which express human ACE2 under the epithelial cytokeratin-18 (KRT18) promoter (Winkler et al., 2020).
evidence: Citation to study describing KRT18-hACE2 mice.

claim: KRT18-hACE2 mice are overly susceptible and develop deadly SARS-CoV-2 encephalitis in addition to pneumonia due to nonphysiological and broad overexpression of hACE2.
source: However, KRT18-hACE2 mice are overly susceptible as they develop deadly SARS-CoV-2 encephalitis (in addition to pneumonia) in response to low infection doses due to nonphysiological and broad (over)expression of hACE2 (Kumari et al., 2021).
evidence: Citation to study describing limitations of KRT18-hACE2 model.

claim: Four mouse-adapted SARS-CoV-2 strains have been generated by either genetic engineering and/or serial passaging.
source: Recently, four mouse-adapted SARS-CoV-2 strains have been generated by either genetic engineering (Dinnon et al., 2020) and/or serial passaging (Gu et al., 2020; Huang et al., 2021; Leist et al., 2020).
evidence: Citations to studies describing other mouse-adapted SARS-CoV-2 strains.

claim: While infectivity is achieved with all mouse-adapted SARS-CoV-2 strains, only two cause pathology that mimics human disease.
source: However, while infectivity is achieved with all of these strains, only two (Huang et al., 2021; Leist et al., 2020) cause a pathology that mimics human disease, and pathological mechanisms are still poorly understood.
evidence: Citations to studies with mouse-adapted strains and assessment of their pathogenicity.

claim: The VOCs Beta/B.1.351 and Gamma/P1 have been found to productively replicate in mice without causing pneumonia.
source: Of note, the VOCs Beta/B.1.351 (Tegally et al., 2020) and Gamma/P1 Voloch, 2020 have been recently found to productively replicate in mice without causing pneumonia (Montagutelli et al., 2021)
evidence: Citation to study showing VOC replication in mice.

claim: Weight loss is a sign of disease severity in many rodent models of infection and related to anorexia and/or cachexia.
source: Weight loss is a sign of disease severity in many rodent models of infection and related to anorexia and/or cachexia (Baazim et al., 2021).
evidence: Citation to study on weight loss as disease indicator in rodent models.

claim: The drop in body temperature in mice infected with passage 15 is the regulatory response of mice to severe inflammation at room temperature.
source: Mice infected with passage 15 furthermore exhibited a severe drop in body temperature (Figure 1D), which is the regulatory response of mice to severe inflammation at room temperature (Garami et al., 2018).
evidence: Body temperature data (Figure 1D) and citation to study on thermoregulation in mice.

claim: The Q498H mutation was intentionally introduced using an engineering approach by the Baric group in an earlier attempt to increase mouse specificity of SARS-CoV-2.
source: This increased mouse infectivity coincided with the appearance of a Spike protein mutation at position 498, which was intentionally introduced using an engineering approach by the Baric group in an earlier attempt to increase mouse specificity of SARS-CoV-2 (Dinnon et al., 2020).
evidence: Citation to Baric group study on engineered mouse-adapted virus.

claim: The Q493R mutation was found in the mouse-adapted variant of the engineered virus after 10 passages through BALB/c mice and reported to improve Spike-mAce2 interaction.
source: Interestingly, another maVie16 Spike protein mutation (at position 493) was also found in the mouse-adapted variant of the engineered virus after 10 passages through BALB/c mice (Gu et al., 2020; Huang et al., 2021; Leist et al., 2020) and reported to improve Spike-mAce2 interaction (Adams et al., 2021).
evidence: Citations to studies on Q493R mutation in other mouse-adapted strains.

claim: Q498H or Q493R mutations had been only sporadically observed in a few patient samples (16 and 196, respectively, according to the GISAID database) until recently.
source: In support of their apparent mouse specificity, Q498H or Q493R mutations had been only sporadically observed in a few patient samples (16 and 196, respectively, according to the GISAID database; Shu and McCauley, 2017) until recently.
evidence: Reference to GISAID database showing rarity of these mutations in human samples.

claim: The Omicron/B.1.1.529 variant harbors the Q493R mutation and Q498R mutation.
source: However, the most recent VOC Omicron/B.1.1.529 harbors the same Q493R mutation and in addition contains Q498R, which leads to the introduction of a basic amino acid (arginine), similar to maVie16's Q498H mutation.
evidence: Reference to Omicron variant sequence.

claim: The K417T Spike protein mutation was found in the Gamma/P1 SARS-CoV-2 VOC.
source: The K417T Spike protein mutation was also found in the Gamma/P1 SARS-CoV-2 VOC (Voloch, 2020)
evidence: Citation to study characterizing Gamma/P1 variant.

claim: K417 was changed to asparagine (K417N) in the Omicron/B1.1.529 and Beta/B.1.351 VOCs.
source: and the same lysine was changed to an asparagine in the Omicron/B1.1.529 and the Beta/B.1.351 VOC (Tegally et al., 2020).
evidence: Citation to study characterizing Beta variant and reference to Omicron.

claim: Beta/B.1.351 and Gamma/P1 SARS-CoV-2 have been shown to replicate in laboratory mice.
source: Importantly, Beta/B.1.351 and Gamma/P1 SARS-CoV-2 have been shown to replicate in laboratory mice (Montagutelli et al., 2021)
evidence: Citation to study showing VOC replication in mice.

claim: In Beta/B.1.351 and Gamma/P1, K417T/N was exclusively observed in conjunction with the mutations N501Y and E484K.
source: and in both K417T/N was exclusively observed in conjunction with the mutations N501Y and E484K.
evidence: Reference to variant sequences showing mutation combinations.

claim: N501Y is suspected to boost SARS-CoV-2 infectivity.
source: While N501Y is suspected to boost infectivity, E484K might contribute to antibody escape and immune evasion.
evidence: Reference to studies on variant mutations and their effects.

claim: E484K might contribute to antibody escape and immune evasion.
source: While N501Y is suspected to boost infectivity, E484K might contribute to antibody escape and immune evasion.
evidence: Reference to studies on variant mutations and their effects.

claim: In its interaction with hACE2, E484 is postulated to form a salt bridge with K31 in hACE2, while the neighboring D30 interacts with K417.
source: In its interaction with hACE2, E484 is postulated to form a salt bridge with K31 in hACE2, while the neighboring D30 interacts with K417.
evidence: Reference to structural studies of Spike-ACE2 interactions.

claim: Mutating K417 and E484 leads to an intramolecular salt bridge between D30 and K31 in hACE2, having only minor effects on receptor interaction.
source: Mutating K417 and E484 leads to an intramolecular salt bridge between D30 and K31 in hACE2, having only minor effects on receptor interaction (Cheng et al., 2021).
evidence: Citation to structural study on variant mutations.

claim: The multibasic S1/S2 furin cleavage site (681-PRRAR) and the S2′ cleavage site (at 815R) were maintained in maVie16.
source: At the same time, the multibasic S1/S2 furin cleavage site (681-PRRAR) as well as the S2′ cleavage site (at 815R) were maintained
evidence: Sequencing data showing conservation of cleavage sites.

claim: TMPRSS2 and furin are highly conserved between mice and men.
source: rendering maVie16 Spike accessible for proteolytic processing by endogenous proteases such as TMPRSS2 or furin, which are essential for productive infection (Takeda, 2022) and highly conserved between mice and men (Vaarala et al., 2001).
evidence: Citation to study on protease conservation.

claim: The co-appearance of Q493 and Q498 mutations in the Omicron/B.1.1.529 variant and maVie16 supports the idea of Omicron being the result of reverse zoonosis and viral evolution in an animal reservoir.
source: In light of the debate about the origin of Omicron/B.1.1.529, we believe that our data, in particular the co-appearance of Q493 and Q498 mutations in the Omicron/B.1.1.529 variant and maVie16, support the idea of Omicron being the result of reverse zoonosis and viral evolution in an animal reservoir (Kupferschmidt, 2021).
evidence: Comparison of mutation patterns and citation to discussion of Omicron origin.

claim: The time to symptom onset in maVie16-infected mice was approximately 2–3 days, which is faster than reported in humans (around 5 days).
source: The time to symptom onset was approximately 2–3 days, which is faster than reported in humans (around 5 days) (Li et al., 2020) and might be explained by the route of infection and subsequent high viral dose in the lower airways, as opposed to droplet infection of the upper respiratory tract in humans.
evidence: Comparison of disease kinetics between mice and humans with citation to human data.

claim: IFNs play an ambiguous role during COVID-19.
source: However, as others have shown that IFNs play an ambiguous role during COVID-19 (Israelow et al., 2020), further experiments (e.g., using IFNAR1-deficient animals or type I IFN blocking antibodies) will be required to address the direct impact of type I IFNs on maVie16 clearance in vivo.
evidence: Citation to study on IFN role in COVID-19.

claim: A detrimental role for cytokines, specifically IFNγ and TNF, had been previously associated with severe COVID-19.
source: A detrimental role for cytokines, specifically IFNγ and TNF, had been previously associated with severe COVID-19 and experimentally identified as a risk factor for severe disease in SARS-CoV-2-infected KRT18-hACE2 mice by causing a form of inflammatory cell death termed PANoptosis (Karki et al., 2021).
evidence: Citation to study on cytokine-driven pathology in COVID-19.

claim: IFNγ and TNF cause a form of inflammatory cell death termed PANoptosis in SARS-CoV-2-infected KRT18-hACE2 mice.
source: A detrimental role for cytokines, specifically IFNγ and TNF, had been previously associated with severe COVID-19 and experimentally identified as a risk factor for severe disease in SARS-CoV-2-infected KRT18-hACE2 mice by causing a form of inflammatory cell death termed PANoptosis (Karki et al., 2021).
evidence: Citation to study describing PANoptosis in COVID-19 model.

claim: Studies based on crystallography, modeling, or in vitro experiments propose ACE2 as the main entry receptor for SARS-CoV-2.
source: Several studies based on crystallography (Wrapp et al., 2020; Yan et al., 2020), modeling (Rodrigues et al., 2020), or in vitro experiments (Cai et al., 2021; Hoffmann et al., 2020; Monteil et al., 2020) propose ACE2 as the main entry receptor for SARS-CoV-2.
evidence: Citations to multiple studies using different approaches to identify ACE2 as receptor.

claim: Experiments using KRT18-hACE2 mice or viral vector-mediated hACE2 delivery systems have shown that ACE2 expression is sufficient for SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: The relevance of ACE2 is further supported by in vivo experiments using KRT18-hACE2 mice (Oladunni et al., 2020) or viral vector-mediated hACE2 delivery systems (Rathnasinghe et al., 2020). Although these experiments have shown that ACE2 expression is sufficient for infection, definitive proof of an essential in vivo role of ACE2 in COVID-19 has not been provided so far.
evidence: Citations to studies using ACE2-expressing mice.

claim: Additional receptors have been proposed that could permit SARS-CoV2 infections, including neuropilin-1 and CD147.
source: This is of particular importance because additional receptors have been proposed that could also permit SARS-CoV2 infections (Cantuti-Castelvetri et al., 2020; Daly et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020b).
evidence: Citations to studies proposing alternative receptors.

claim: A genome-wide association study across more than 50,000 COVID-19 patients and more than 700,000 noninfected individuals revealed a rare variant associated with downregulated ACE2 expression and reduced risk of COVID-19.
source: A recently published genome-wide association study across more than 50,000 COVID-19 patients and more than 700,000 noninfected individuals revealed a rare variant that was associated with downregulated ACE2 expression and reduced risk of COVID-19 (Horowitz et al., 2021), providing additional evidence for the importance of ACE2 for SARS-CoV-2 infection in humans.
evidence: Citation to GWAS study linking ACE2 to COVID-19 risk.

claim: Recombinant human soluble ACE2 slowed SARS-CoV-2 viral replication in organoids.
source: The principal effectiveness of recombinant human soluble (rhs) ACE2 towards SARS-CoV-2 was demonstrated earlier in organoids as it slowed viral replication in this setting (Monteil et al., 2020).
evidence: Citation to study showing ACE2 effect on viral replication in organoids.

claim: It has been proposed that soluble ACE2 might enhance SARS-CoV-2 infections, but the maVie16 data do not support this.
source: It has been recently proposed that soluble ACE2 might enhance SARS-CoV-2 infections (Yeung et al., 2021), however, our data do not support this.
evidence: Citation to contrasting study and reference to own experimental results.

claim: Different forms of ACE2 can protect from disease in hamsters and KRT18-hACE2 mouse models.
source: Moreover, using hamsters (Higuchi et al., 2021; Linsky et al., 2020) and the KRT18-hACE2 mouse model (Hassler et al., 2021), it has also been shown that different forms of ACE2 can protect from disease
evidence: Citations to studies showing protective effects of ACE2 in animal models.

claim: Recombinant human soluble ACE2 is being tested in clinical trials in COVID-19 patients with first promising results.
source: RhsACE2, prepared in the same way as rmsACE2 we used for our inhalation experiments (Monteil et al., 2020), is now being tested in clinical trials in COVID-19 patients with first promising results (Zoufaly et al., 2020).
evidence: Citations to clinical trial reports on ACE2 therapy.

claim: Variants that can escape vaccine efficacy and approved antibody therapies have been selected for better ACE2 binding.
source: Considering the emergence of variants that can escape in part vaccine efficacy and approved antibody therapies (Yuan et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2021) and the fact that these variants have been apparently selected for better ACE2 binding (Tian et al., 2021; Yuan et al., 2021)
evidence: Citations to studies on variant evolution and ACE2 binding.

claim: ACE2 inhalation has the potential to prevent or treat early stages of SARS-CoV-2 infections irrespective of the virus variant.
source: ACE2 inhalation has the potential to prevent or treat early stages of SARS-CoV-2 infections irrespective of the virus variant. However, whether inhalable ACE2 indeed constitutes a universal strategy against current and future SARS-CoV-2 variants needs careful testing in clinical trials.
evidence: Inference from experimental data and discussion of therapeutic potential.

claim: Infectivity was quickly established after the first few passages of BavPat1 in BALB/c mice, as indicated by increasing SARS-CoV-2 genome copies detected in the lungs.
source: Infectivity was quickly established after the first few passages, as indicated by increasing SARS-CoV-2 genome copies detected in the lungs of infected mice (Figure 1B).
evidence: Viral load data from serial passaging shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The viral load did not further change after passage 3 during serial passaging.
source: While the viral load did not further change after passage 3, a progressive loss of body weight of mice infected with later stage passaged SARS-CoV-2 indicated enhanced pathogenicity of the virus (Figure 1C).
evidence: Viral load data shown in Figure 1B showing plateau after passage 3.

claim: Progressive loss of body weight of mice infected with later stage passaged SARS-CoV-2 indicated enhanced pathogenicity of the virus.
source: While the viral load did not further change after passage 3, a progressive loss of body weight of mice infected with later stage passaged SARS-CoV-2 indicated enhanced pathogenicity of the virus (Figure 1C).
evidence: Body weight data from serial passaging shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The transcriptional analysis of pulmonary inflammatory genes revealed a progressively increasing inflammatory response during serial passaging.
source: The transcriptional analysis of pulmonary inflammatory genes (including Il1b, Ifng, Il6, and Tnf) 3 days after infection with the different passages revealed a progressively increasing inflammatory response (Figure 1E).
evidence: Gene expression data from serial passaging shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Despite substantially increased virulence in mice, only a limited number of mutations with high allele frequencies were found in maVie16, located in the Spike protein, ORF1AB, and envelope.
source: Despite the substantially increased virulence in mice, we found only a limited number of mutations with high (>0.5) allele frequencies, located in the Spike protein, open reading frame (ORF)1AB, and envelope (Figure 2A).
evidence: Sequencing data showing mutation distribution in Figure 2A.

claim: Three de novo mutations were found within the Spike receptor binding domain (RBD) of maVie16.
source: Given the importance of Spike for SARS-CoV-2 infectivity, we were particularly interested in the three de novo mutations within its receptor binding domain (RBD) (Figure 2B).
evidence: Sequencing data showing RBD mutations in Figure 2B.

claim: The observed Spike mutations in maVie16 are distant from putative cleavage sites, suggesting mACE2 affinity is increased without affecting proteolytic processing.
source: Since the observed Spike mutations are distant from putative cleavage sites (Takeda, 2022), it is likely that mACE2 affinity is increased without affecting proteolytic processing by proteases such as furin or TMPRSS2 (Takeda, 2022).
evidence: Structural analysis and citation to study on cleavage sites.

claim: Both simian and human cells continue to serve as useful tools for maVie16 propagation and titer determination.
source: Thus, while the interaction with mACE2 is enhanced, the infectivity of human cells remained unchanged for maVie16 and both simian and human cells continue to serve as a useful tool for maVie16 propagation and titer determination.
evidence: In vitro propagation data showing similar growth in Vero and Caco-2 cells.

claim: pDCs are important antiviral effector cells capable of efficient and rapid type I IFN production.
source: At the same time, we observed an expansion of peripheral plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDCs) (Figure 4B), which are important antiviral effector cells capable of efficient and rapid type I IFN production (Swiecki and Colonna, 2015).
evidence: Citation to study on pDC function.

claim: T cells are prominent sources of IFNγ.
source: The Ifng induction reached a maximum on day 7, coinciding with the increased numbers of T cells that are prominent sources of IFNγ (Figure 4D).
evidence: Established immunological knowledge about T cell cytokine production.
